This plan turns Design into a first-class phase in the same way
Implementation already is — its own gate, its own agent role, its
own tab — while keeping papercusp generic enough to design React,
Rust, C++, or anything else with a UI.

Earlier discussion lived in chat; this doc is the canonical spec
for the build.

---

# 1. Why a phase, not a tag

Tags are orthogonal grouping (which features share memory). Phases
are sequential states with gates and deliverables. Design has both.
Every feature with a user-facing surface needs design *before*
implementation, then again as *review* after; that's a workflow,
not a label.

A separate Design tab is justified because the working surface is
different from the dashboard's: queues, mocks, tokens, registry,
visual diff. The data spine is shared with the dashboard's Features
component (see §6).

---

# 2. Lifecycle integration

Design reuses the existing card lifecycle vocabulary
(`pending / accepted / ignored`). It does not introduce new state
names. The phase is the axis of difference, not the state machine.

A feature record gains:

```
needsDesign:         boolean    // set by orchestrator on creation
designStatus:        Lifecycle  // pending | accepted | ignored
designSpec:          SpecRef|null  // pointer to spec when accepted
discardedDesignWork: boolean    // human force-skipped after work began
```

`pending` covers both "awaiting designer spawn" and "designer in
flight" — the implementation lifecycle treats spawned-but-unfinished
the same way.

`ignored` is overloaded: it can mean "phase explicitly skipped"
(this feature doesn't need design) or "feature dropped" (no design
will happen because the feature is dead). The two are conflated
because the gate behavior is identical (no spec required to advance
or close). If telemetry needs to distinguish, use the existing
feature-lifecycle status to disambiguate.

Gate: a feature cannot transition into the implementing phase until
`designStatus ∈ { accepted, ignored }`.

## 2.1 Storage

> **As shipped:** the lifecycle fields landed as **columns on the existing
> canonical features table** rather than a new sibling table — `needs_design`,
> `design_status`, `design_spec_id`, `discarded_design_work` on
> `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated`, keyed by
> `(harness_slug, feature_id)`. There is no `harness_design_phase` table; the
> gate reads the design columns straight from the consolidated store.

`needsDesign`, `designStatus`, `designSpec`, `discardedDesignWork`
live on the canonical features table
`harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated` (columns
`needs_design`, `design_status`, `design_spec_id`,
`discarded_design_work`), keyed by `(harness_slug, feature_id)`, in
the harness DB. This matches the existing pattern (per memory:
features, issues, proposals, etc., are PG-canonical via Zero sync).

Spec artifacts (the IR JSON, sketches, screenshots) live in a
sibling table `harness_shared.harness_design_artifacts` with columns
`(id, harness_slug, feature_id, kind, payload, metadata,
created_ts)`, keyed by `(harness_slug, id)`. (Note the `created_ts`
BIGINT timestamp, and the `id` + `metadata` columns the earlier draft
omitted.) PG over filesystem so artifacts are queryable, syncable via
Zero, and survive harness moves.

## 2.2 Relationship to existing `proposals`

Design specs are NOT proposals. Proposals (per memory) are
implementation alternatives — competing plans for how to build
something. Design specs define what to build. Sibling category,
new table, no overloading.

A proposal MAY reference a design spec; a design spec NEVER
references a proposal.

---

# 3. The `needsDesign` heuristic

Cheap, deterministic, runs at feature creation. Falsy means skip
the design phase entirely.

The heuristic reads from the *proposal/scope* — feature description,
acceptance criteria, plan text, declared file globs — not from
actual code diffs (there are none at creation time).

```
needsDesign := proposalMentionsUiSurface
            || proposalMentionsUserCopy
            || proposalDeclaresNewRoute
            || proposalDeclaresIconography
            || proposalGlobsMatchUiPaths   // declared file globs
            || flaggedManually
```

Where `uiPaths` is per-ecosystem-adapter (React-Tailwind: `**/*.tsx
/ **/*.css`; Qt: `**/*.ui / **/*.qml`; etc.). Adapters declare
their UI globs; the orchestrator unions across active adapters.

Backend, infra, refactors, and bugfixes skip by default. The
orchestrator can override either direction.

---

# 4. Roles

## 4.1 Designer agent

Output is a *specification*, not edited components. To enforce
this, the runtime restricts designer commits to a per-adapter
allowlist (default: `design/`, `apps/operator-docs/src/content/docs/design/`, sketch
artifact paths). Commits outside the allowlist are rejected with a
clear error and the designer is re-prompted, not killed.

If a designer legitimately needs to scaffold something outside the
allowlist (e.g., a token JSON proposal in a custom path), the
designer requests an allowlist extension via a special spec
annotation; orchestrator (or human) approves.

Deliverables per feature:

- A UI IR document (see §7) describing the surface
- Token decisions (which existing tokens, any new ones — §9)
- Component contract: which registry components to use, with which
  variants and props
- Copy (labels, empty states, error messages)
- Interaction states (hover/focus/disabled/loading/error)
- Optional: tldraw sketch, screenshot annotations, references

Inputs:

- The feature record (description, acceptance criteria)
- `DESIGN_SPEC.md` (global rules — §5; with fallback chain)
- Component registry (§8)
- Token store (§9)
- Adjacent design memos under `apps/operator-docs/src/content/docs/design/`
- **For redesigns of existing features:** preview-adapter capture
  of the current state (screenshot or live preview URL); designer
  needs to know what exists before proposing changes

## 4.2 Design reviewer (lightweight)

After implementation ships, a review pass compares the rendered
surface to the spec. Output is either *approved* or a re-opened
design card with the diff.

If the reviewer rejects, a fresh designer agent is spawned with:
the rejected spec, the rendered diff, and the reviewer's notes as
new input. The original designer's spec is preserved as an artifact
for traceability — never overwritten.

Reviewer is the same agent persona as the designer with a
different prompt; one binary, two roles.

## 4.3 Orchestrator changes

Concrete trigger for spawning designers:

```
designReady := needsDesign
            && designStatus == null
            && dependencies.allMet
            && scope.stable
            && !backoff.active   // see below
```

After a rejected design, a back-off timer prevents immediate
re-spawn (default 1 hour, configurable). Rejection reasons feed
the next prompt so the designer doesn't repeat the mistake.

The orchestrator also:

- Sets `needsDesign` on creation per heuristic (§3)
- Spawns the appropriate number of designers (§20.9)
- Honors the gate before promoting to implementing
- Schedules the post-ship review pass

## 4.4 Cost / token budget

Designers spawn 2–3 per feature (§20.9) and consume tokens on a
similar order to implementers. Budget controls are the same as
implementers — orchestrator can drop to N=1 for cost-constrained
features, and the global per-workspace budget cap covers both
designer and implementer spend. No separate budget axis.

---

# 5. `DESIGN_SPEC.md`

A separate doc, sibling to `SPEC.md`, that the designer agent
always loads. Contents:

- Voice, tone, terminology rules
- Token policy (when to use existing vs propose new)
- Accessibility minimums
- Animation / motion rules (already partially captured in
  `/docs/design/performance` and `libraries`)
- Forbidden patterns (anti-pattern catalog)
- Approved component list (links into §8)

## 5.1 Fallback chain

Resolved in order; first hit wins:

1. `<harness root>/DESIGN_SPEC.md`
2. `<workspace root>/DESIGN_SPEC.md`
3. `<papercusp app default>/DESIGN_SPEC.md` (ships with the SDK,
   minimal — just "use existing tokens, semantic HTML, ARIA roles")
4. Empty (with a logged warning surfaced as a banner in the design
   tab: "no DESIGN_SPEC.md found; using minimal defaults")

Day-1 is unblocked by (3). Harnesses adopt their own as needed.

## 5.2 Per-harness scope

This file is per-harness, not per-workspace, so different harnesses
(different surfaces, different teams, different ecosystems) carry
different design rules without contaminating each other. Designer
agent loads the spec from the active harness root.

---

# 6. The Design tab

Add a sibling to the Dashboard tab. The existing Features component
takes a `mode` parameter; default is `dashboard`, design tab passes
`design`. Mode controls:

- Which columns render (design adds: design status chip, mock link,
  token-decision chip, approval state)
- Which actions appear (design adds: open spec, open mocks,
  approve, request changes, mark skipped)
- Which sub-filter buckets exist (design uses: needs-design /
  in-design / approved / skipped / review-pending)

## 6.1 Pane layout

Three-column layout, mirroring the dashboard's overall feel:

- **Left rail** — Features list (the shared component in
  `mode=design`), filterable by sub-bucket
- **Main column** — the active pane (one of the six below);
  pane-switcher tabs across the top
- **Right rail** — selected feature detail (spec, status, recent
  events, designer/reviewer assignments)

Six panes for the main column:

1. **Features (mode=design)** — shared component (also lives in
   the left rail; tab repeats it for full-width view)
2. **Design memos** — surface `apps/operator-docs/src/content/docs/design/*.mdx` as a
   working backlog with status (open / addressed / wontfix)
3. **Component registry browser** — searchable inventory (§8);
   humans browse, agents query via MCP
4. **Token inventory** — DTCG store (§9), with per-ecosystem
   preview of generated outputs
5. **Sketch / annotation canvas** — embedded tldraw, scoped to the
   selected feature
6. **Visual regression strip** — Lost Pixel screenshots,
   before/after per route or per component

A seventh, deferred: cross-app consistency audit (operator vs
papercup vs papercusp). Defer until tokens are unified.

## 6.2 Approval actor model

- **Reviewer agent** approves or rejects by default after
  implementation ships
- **Human** can approve or reject at any time, including before
  the reviewer agent runs — explicit human approval bypasses the
  agent
- **Designer agent** never self-approves
- Approve / Reject actions are visible on the feature card in
  both Dashboard and Design tabs

## 6.3 Operator-panel integration

Design events surface in the OperatorPanel directive cards (per
the existing pattern) when they need user attention:

- Design crit deadlocked — needs human pick
- Designer escalated (failure-mode TBD per §18)
- Reviewer rejected, re-spawn requires confirm
- New token proposed, awaiting approval

In-flight states (designer running, awaiting dependency) stay
internal — they go in the design-tab events column, not as
operator directives, to avoid card noise.

---

# 7. The UI IR — JSON shape, ecosystem-agnostic

This is the most important architectural decision in the plan.

The designer agent emits a *semantic* tree that implementer
adapters resolve into their idioms. It must not emit JSX, Tailwind
classes, Qt XML, or any ecosystem-specific syntax.

## 7.1 Why JSON, not a custom DSL

We considered copying Slint's syntax (a real declarative DSL with
parser/typechecker/LSP) versus a JSON schema. JSON wins
unambiguously because the IR's primary author and primary consumer
are both LLMs:

| | DSL (Slint-like) | JSON IR |
|---|---|---|
| Time to v0.1 | 3–4 months | 2–3 weeks |
| LLM emission quality | Mid; needs many-shot | Native |
| Free tooling | None (write parser/LSP/diff) | jq, JSON Patch, JSON Schema, IDE support |
| Adapter complexity | Parse → AST → walk | Consume object directly |
| Refactoring cost | Touches parser + adapters | Bump `irVersion`, ship transformer |

A DSL's main benefit (human readability) doesn't apply when humans
aren't the primary authors. Costs (parser, LSP, agent prompt
overhead, two-layer adapter parsing) all do.

**Hybrid escape hatch (Vega-Lite/Altair pattern):** if a real
human-authoring use case ever emerges, ship a thin DSL surface
that compiles to the same JSON. We never lose the option.

## 7.2 Schema language: JSON Schema (default), CUE (option)

JSON Schema is universally understood and trivial to validate in
every language. **CUE** is stronger — real type system, better
constraint expression — and is worth considering once the IR
stabilizes. Start with JSON Schema; migrate to CUE if/when limits
bite.

## 7.3 Sketch of the shape (illustrative — valid JSON in v0.1
examples)

```jsonc
{
  "irVersion": "0.1",
  "surface": "operator-panel",
  "ecosystem": "*",
  "layout": {
    "kind": "stack",
    "direction": "vertical",
    "gap": { "token": "space.md" },
    "children": [
      { "kind": "header", "title": { "copy": "Operator" } },
      {
        "kind": "list",
        "emptyState": { "copy": "No directives.", "icon": "inbox" },
        "item": {
          "kind": "card",
          "slots": {
            "title":   { "ref": "card.title" },
            "body":    { "ref": "card.body" },
            "actions": { "ref": "card.actions" }
          },
          "interactions": ["hover", "focus", "select"]
        }
      }
    ]
  },
  "components": [
    {
      "id": "btn-accept",
      "registry": "action.primary",
      "props": { "label": "Accept" }
    }
  ],
  "tokens": {
    "uses": ["color.bg.surface", "color.fg.primary", "space.md", "radius.sm"]
  },
  "states": {
    "loading": { "kind": "spinner", "label": { "copy": "Loading…" } },
    "error":   { "copy": "Could not load directives.", "retry": true }
  },
  "a11y": { "landmark": "main", "headingLevel": 2 }
}
```

Properties of this format:

- No DOM assumptions. `kind: "stack"` becomes flexbox, QVBoxLayout,
  or `Vertical { }` depending on adapter.
- No CSS. Visual properties reference tokens, never literals.
- No imperative JS. Interactions are declared by name; adapters
  bind them.
- Explicit registry references for non-primitive components.
- `kind` values draw from OpenUI vocabulary
  (`open-ui.org/components`) where possible, so naming aligns with
  industry usage.

## 7.4 Sub-IR escape hatch — Plotly for charts

Charts are a domain that already has a mature multi-language
declarative spec. We don't reinvent it.

```jsonc
{ "kind": "chart", "spec": { /* Plotly JSON */ } }
```

Designer agent reaches for `kind: "chart"` only when the surface
genuinely includes data viz; otherwise compose primitives.

**Plotly** chosen over Vega-Lite, ECharts, ApexCharts after survey:

- Most language bindings of any chart spec — JS, Python, R, Julia,
  MATLAB, F#, .NET. Directly serves the cross-ecosystem goal.
- Most LLM training data (pervasive in data-science notebooks);
  agents emit it more reliably.
- Verbose but explicit; agents don't care about character count,
  and explicit specs are easier to validate and diff.
- 18.2k★, large active community.

Vega-Lite's grammar-of-graphics elegance matters when humans
compose specs by hand — wrong axis to optimize for an
agent-authored format.

## 7.5 No card / form sub-IR

Earlier drafts proposed embedding Adaptive Cards as a card sub-IR.
On closer look, AC's unique value is its multi-stack *external*
renderer ecosystem (Teams, Outlook actionable messages, Bot
Framework). For *our internal* cards/forms/dashboards, embedding
AC adds a dependency without saving work and constrains us to AC's
bounded vocabulary.

The IR's general `kind: "card"` / `kind: "form"` is rendered by
the ecosystem adapter. Adapters may *implement* their renderer
using libraries like JSON Forms, react-jsonschema-form, or Formily
— that's an adapter detail, not an IR-level decision.

Adaptive Cards reappears in §13 as an *export adapter*, not a
sub-IR.

## 7.6 Iconography

Icons are a sub-registry under the component registry, with their
own schema (`iconId → svgPath / sourcePointer`). Referenced by ID
in the IR. As shipped in v0.1 the IR's icon reference is a **plain
string id** (`iconRef = string`): the inline slot-prop form is
`"icon": "inbox"`, and the `{ kind: "icon", id: "inbox" }` node form
carries the same string under its `icon` field. Adapters scan icon
paths declared in their manifest; the React-Tailwind adapter will
scan `lucide-react` exports + project-local SVGs.

## 7.7 Copy and i18n

Every user-facing string in the IR uses `{ key, default }`:

```jsonc
{ "title": { "key": "operator.header.title", "default": "Operator" } }
```

Adapters that have no i18n runtime treat `default` as the literal.
Adapters with i18n (most React apps) wire `key` through their
existing translation layer. Designers default to `key`-with-default
on every spec — cheap now, prohibitively expensive to retrofit.

## 7.8 Responsive / viewport

Layout nodes accept per-breakpoint overrides keyed by named
viewport tokens (`viewport.narrow`, `viewport.medium`,
`viewport.wide`) defined in the DTCG store:

```jsonc
{
  "kind": "stack",
  "direction": "vertical",
  "responsive": {
    "viewport.wide": { "direction": "horizontal" }
  }
}
```

Container-query semantics — overrides apply when the *container*
matches the viewport, not the global window. Adapter resolves to
its idiomatic mechanism (CSS container queries, Qt layout
policies, etc.).

## 7.9 Theming (light/dark, brand variants)

The IR always references base token IDs. Theme resolution is the
adapter's job, driven by the active DTCG `$themes` group. Designer
never thinks about light/dark in the spec; they think about
semantic tokens (`color.bg.surface`) that resolve correctly under
any theme.

## 7.10 Motion / animation

A `motion` field on layout/component nodes declares intent
semantically:

```jsonc
{ "motion": { "enter": "slide-up", "exit": "fade", "duration": "duration.md" } }
```

Allowed values draw from a small, named vocabulary — the shipped
schema enum is `fade / slide-up / slide-down / slide-left /
slide-right / scale / none`. Concrete keyframes/easings live in
tokens (`duration.*`, `easing.*`).
Adapters bind to their motion library (motion / auto-animate / Qt
animations / etc.).

## 7.11 A11y — per-element

`a11y` lives on every interactive node, not just the surface root:

```jsonc
{
  "kind": "button",
  "registry": "action.primary",
  "props": { "label": { "key": "...", "default": "Accept" } },
  "a11y": {
    "role": "button",
    "ariaLabel": { "key": "...", "default": "Accept directive" },
    "keyboardShortcut": "Enter"
  }
}
```

The surface root keeps `landmark` + `headingLevel`. Live regions,
focus management, and tab order get dedicated fields as the IR
matures (open: do these go in `a11y` or a sibling `interaction`
field?).

## 7.12 Composition: surface vs route

A *surface* is one IR document. A *route* is a thin manifest that
lists surfaces (and their layout — split-pane, tabs, modal stack).
Route manifests are a separate JSON shape, much smaller than
surface IR. Designer authors a route spec when adding/changing
navigation; otherwise just surfaces.

## 7.13 Data binding boundary

The IR declares slots and binding points; it does not declare data
sources. A list says "this is a list, items repeat, each item gets
slots A B C"; the implementer wires the data source.

```jsonc
{
  "kind": "list",
  "binding": { "slot": "items", "repeats": true, "shape": "DirectiveCard" },
  "item": { /* IR for one item, slots reference DirectiveCard fields */ }
}
```

`shape` is a named type the implementer maps to its data layer
(TypeScript type, Rust struct, etc.). The designer doesn't pick
the data source; the implementer does.

## 7.14 Free-form escape hatch

When the IR genuinely can't express something, `kind: "raw"` lets
the designer hand off ecosystem-native code:

```jsonc
{ "kind": "raw", "ecosystem": "react-tailwind", "payload": "<MyJsx/>" }
```

Linter flags `raw` as a warning (it bypasses the abstraction);
crit may reject if used to skip thinking. Always available, never
default.

## 7.15 IR linter (anti-pattern checks)

A validator says "is this valid JSON matching the schema?". A
linter says "is this *good* IR?". Both run on every submitted
spec. Lint rules (open-ended, expand as patterns emerge):

- Maximum nesting depth (default 6)
- Every interactive element has an `a11y.role` or maps to a
  registry component that supplies one
- No literal colors / dimensions outside `tokens.uses` references
- Every `states.error` has a recovery action (retry, navigate)
- Every `states.loading` has an aria-live equivalent
- `surface` is unique within the harness
- Registry component IDs all resolve in the active registry
- Token IDs all resolve in the active DTCG store

Linter runs at submit time; warnings flow to the design crit
prompt; errors block acceptance until fixed.

# 8. Component registry — neutral schema + ecosystem adapters

shadcn's registry is React/Tailwind-coupled. We want the *idea*
without the coupling.

## 8.1 Neutral schema

```jsonc
{
  "id": "action.primary",            // semantic id, ecosystem-free
  "kind": "component",
  "summary": "Primary call-to-action button",
  "inputs": [
    { "name": "label", "type": "string", "required": true },
    { "name": "icon",  "type": "icon",   "required": false }
  ],
  "variants": ["default", "loading", "disabled"],
  "states":   ["hover", "focus", "active"],
  "examples": [{ "inputs": { "label": "Accept" }, "preview": "asset:..." }],
  "ecosystems": {
    "react-tailwind": {
      "sourcePointer": "<adapter-declared-path>/Button.tsx",
      "importHint":    "import { Button } from '...'",
      "propMap":       { "label": "children", "icon": "leftIcon" }
    },
    "qt-widgets":  { "sourcePointer": "...", "importHint": "...", "propMap": {} }
  }
}
```

Designer agent searches by semantic id / summary / inputs.
Implementer agent (which already knows its ecosystem) reads the
matching `ecosystems[e]` block to know what to import and how to
map props.

## 8.2 Registry adapters

Adapters populate the registry by scanning paths they themselves
declare — no global hardcoded path.

- `registry-adapter-react-shadcn` — scans the React/TSX path tree
  declared in the adapter manifest; infers inputs from TS prop
  types; captures Storybook screenshots as examples. Ships first.
  For papercusp itself, the declared path is `libs/papercusp/`.
- `registry-adapter-qt-widgets` — community
- `registry-adapter-egui` — community
- `registry-adapter-slint` — community

Adapters are papercusp plugins (we already have a plugin system).

## 8.3 Cross-harness sharing

The registry is per-harness because each harness has its own
component path tree. For shared design system libraries (e.g., a
papercup-org-wide `libs/papercusp/` that multiple harnesses
consume), the adapter manifest can declare additional registry
sources outside the harness root. Cross-harness registry sharing
is opt-in per adapter, not implicit.

---

# 9. Tokens — DTCG as canonical, per-ecosystem outputs

The W3C Design Tokens Community Group format
(`design-tokens.org`) is the cross-ecosystem standard JSON for
tokens. It is deliberately neutral: color, dimension, typography,
duration, etc.

Adopt DTCG as the canonical token store under `design/tokens/`. As
shipped, the canonical DTCG store file is
**`design/tokens/base.json`** — the runtime sync-resolver, the
`list_tokens` MCP tool, and the Design tab's Token pane all read it
directly. The seeder writes a sibling
`design/tokens/seeded-from-harness-css.json` as the input to the
manual semantic pass (§20.13), which merges into `base.json`.
Per-ecosystem transformers emit:

- CSS custom properties for React/Tauri
- Tailwind preset
- `.qss` for Qt
- Theme structs for egui / iced
- `.slint` for Slint
- Anything the adapter author writes

Transformer choice: **Terrazzo** (DTCG-native, modern) or
**Style Dictionary** (battle-tested, Amazon). Terrazzo is the
recommended default for new code; Style Dictionary remains a fine
choice for adapters that need the wider transform ecosystem.

> **As shipped:** the repo-level `npm run tokens` build runs on
> **Style Dictionary v4** (`^4.4.0`, config in
> `design-tokens/style-dictionary.config.mjs`) — not Terrazzo. The
> react-tailwind adapter, on a separate path, ships its **own minimal
> in-house** CSS-vars + Tailwind-preset emitter (its docstring notes
> Terrazzo "is not yet a dep"). Terrazzo remains the planned long-term
> transformer but is not currently a dependency.

This solves the existing harness.css triplication problem
(operator + libs/papercusp + libs/git-graph) as a side effect:
single source, generated outputs.

## 9.1 Proposing new tokens

When a designer's spec needs a token that doesn't exist:

1. Spec annotates `tokens.proposed: [{ id, type, value, reason }]`
2. Linter flags this as a warning, not an error (proposals are
   normal)
3. Token inventory pane surfaces the proposal as a "review new
   token" action
4. Approver (human or design crit) promotes the proposal into the
   DTCG store, optionally renaming for semantic consistency
5. Spec is re-validated; the token ID resolves; gate can advance

Auto-promotion is off by default — token names are a
human/design-judgment call.

## 9.2 Human authoring paths

- **Tokens Studio for Figma** (Figma plugin) — for designers
  comfortable in Figma; exports DTCG natively
- **Token inventory pane** — custom in-app editor, built into the
  Design tab (§6.4). DTCG JSON is simple enough that per-type
  controls (color picker, dimension input, font dropdown) are a
  small build. There is no mature standalone OSS token editor to
  adopt.
- **tweakcn** — visual editor specifically for the Tailwind
  output; optional, downstream of DTCG.

---

# 10. Preview surface — abstract pane with adapters

Storybook is web-only. Treat it as the React adapter for a generic
*preview pane* concept.

Preview adapter contract:

```
capturePreview({ componentId, variant, state }) -> ImageAsset
listPrimitives() -> ComponentId[]
livePreviewUrl?({ componentId }) -> URL    // optional, web-style only
```

Adapters:

- `preview-adapter-storybook` — for React (mounts existing
  Storybook stories, captures via Playwright)
- `preview-adapter-binary-screenshot` — for native apps; exec the
  binary with a flag, capture the window
- `preview-adapter-slint-live` — Slint's own live preview
- `preview-adapter-headless-imgui` — captures ImGui frames

The Design tab's preview pane is adapter-agnostic; it just renders
whatever asset the active adapter returned.

---

# 11. Sketch / annotate

Embed **tldraw** in the Design tab. Pixels and shapes are
ecosystem-neutral; nothing to abstract.

Sketches are stored in `harness_design_artifacts` (§2.1) with
`kind = "sketch"`, payload = tldraw's serialized state. They're
keyed to the feature, retrievable across sessions, and Zero-synced
to all clients.

Designer agent can also drop annotations on screenshots produced
by the preview adapter (e.g., "this gap should be space.md") —
stored with `kind = "annotation"`.

---

# 12. Visual regression — Lost Pixel

**Lost Pixel** is the OSS Percy/Chromatic alternative; it operates
on screenshots so it works for any ecosystem that can produce a
window. Run on PRs against the previous baseline; surface the diff
strip in the Design tab and as a check on the feature card.

For native ecosystems: the same `capturePreview` adapter that
feeds the preview pane feeds Lost Pixel.

## 12.1 Baseline ownership

- Baseline = last main-branch commit
- PR diffs against that baseline; the strip surfaces every changed
  screenshot
- Explicit "approve diff" action (human or reviewer agent) updates
  the baseline at merge time
- No silent baseline drift; every change is approved

---

# 13. Mock import + external export adapters

## 13.1 Mock-input adapters

Figma is React-world's mock-source default but irrelevant to a Qt
dev. Treat the **Figma-Context-MCP** shape (selection → semantic
tree → component matches) as the *protocol*, with Figma being one
implementation.

- `mock-adapter-figma` — Figma Dev Mode MCP
- `mock-adapter-tldraw` — sketches drawn in the embedded canvas
- `mock-adapter-screenshot` — image → semantic tree
  (uses `screenshot-to-code` style primitive)
- `mock-adapter-text` — pure prose spec

Each adapter declares its `parse(input)` input shape in the plugin
manifest (e.g., Figma adapter expects a Figma node URL; screenshot
adapter expects an image asset). All emit into the same UI IR, so
the designer agent's downstream flow is identical regardless of
input.

## 13.2 External-surface export adapters

When a feature targets an *external* surface that has its own
declarative format and renderer ecosystem, the implementer adapter
emits that format directly from the IR. We don't write renderers
for these surfaces.

- `export-adapter-adaptive-cards` — emits Adaptive Cards JSON for
  Teams, Outlook actionable messages, Bot Framework, Cortana Skills
- `export-adapter-slack-block-kit` — emits Slack Block Kit JSON
  for Slack messages and modals
- `export-adapter-discord-embeds` — community
- (community can add more)

One plugin per export target. Optional and opt-in per feature.

---

# 14. The Ecosystem Adapter Contract

The first concrete artifact to build. Every adapter type listed
above (registry, preview, token output, mock input, code emit,
export) is a specialization of a single plugin shape:

```typescript
interface DesignEcosystemAdapter {
  id:          string;     // stable plugin id, e.g. "papercusp-design-react-tailwind"
  displayName: string;     // human-readable, e.g. "React + Tailwind (papercusp)"
  ecosystem:   string;     // machine ecosystem id; matches the IR `ecosystem` field, e.g. "react-tailwind"
  capabilities: AdapterCapability[];
  irVersionsSupported: string[];    // e.g. ["0.x", "1.x"]
  uiPaths: string[];                // globs for needsDesign heuristic

  registry?: {
    sourcePaths: string[];                          // declared scan roots
    listPrimitives(): RegistryEntry[];
    sourceFor(id: string): SourcePointer;
  };
  preview?: {
    capture(spec: PreviewSpec): Promise<ImageAsset>;
  };
  tokens?: {
    emit(dtcg: DtcgDoc): Promise<FileEmit[]>;
  };
  mockInput?: {
    inputShape: JsonSchema;                         // declared input contract
    parse(input: unknown): Promise<UiIr>;
  };
  codeEmit?: {
    /**
     * @param ir   the spec to emit
     * @param target.outDir destination workspace path
     * @param target.mode   "scaffold" | "patch" | "preview"
     */
    fromIR(ir: UiIr, target: CodeEmitTarget): Promise<FileEmit[]>;
  };
  exportTarget?: {
    targetId: string;                               // "adaptive-cards", ...
    fromIR(ir: UiIr): Promise<unknown>;             // target-native payload
  };
}
```

Ships in the papercusp plugin SDK. The first adapter is
`papercusp-design-react-tailwind`, used by papercusp itself
(eat-your-own-dogfood).

---

# 15. MCP surface for designer agents

Designers consume the registry, tokens, memos, and live surface
state via an MCP server bundled with the design phase. Tools:

- `searchRegistry({ query, ecosystem? }) → RegistryEntry[]`
- `getRegistryComponent(id) → RegistryEntry`
- `readToken(id) → DtcgToken | null`
- `listTokens({ category? }) → DtcgToken[]`
- `proposeToken({ id, type, value, reason }) → ProposalRef`
- `submitSpec(featureId, ir) → { ok, lintIssues, validationErrors }`
- `lintSpec(ir) → LintIssue[]`             — pre-submit self-check
- `validateSpec(ir) → ValidationError[]`   — schema-only check
- `listMemos({ status?, tags? }) → Memo[]`
- `readMemo(slug) → Memo`
- `captureCurrentSurface(featureId) → ImageAsset | null`
- `getDesignSpec() → string`               — the resolved DESIGN_SPEC.md
- `listSiblingSpecs(featureId) → SpecRef[]`  — recent accepted specs
  in the same harness for style consistency

Reviewer/crit get a superset that adds `compareSpecs(a, b)`,
`acceptSpec(featureId, specId)`, `rejectSpec(featureId, specId,
reason)`.

---

# 16. Implementer-side IR consumption

Implementer agents are upgraded to consume IR. Two protocol options
considered; we ship (b) first.

(a) **Code-emit fast path** — adapter's `codeEmit.fromIR()` produces
scaffold files, implementer edits them. Faster but the implementer
loses understanding of *why* code looks the way it does.

(b) **IR-as-context** — implementer prompt includes the IR JSON +
the adapter's "how to translate IR into this ecosystem" rules.
Implementer writes code by hand, referring to IR. Slower per
feature but produces higher-quality, idiomatic code; implementer
internalizes the design intent.

Path (b) is the default. Path (a) is opt-in for high-volume CRUD
features where idiomaticity matters less than throughput.

The implementer prompt gains a section: "the design spec is the
source of truth for what to build; deviations require a new
designer pass, not silent edits."

---

# 17. Testing strategy

- **IR validator** — golden specs that should/shouldn't validate;
  per-rule unit tests
- **IR linter** — per-rule unit tests with positive + negative
  examples
- **Adapter conformance** — the plugin SDK ships an
  `assertAdapterConformant()` test harness any adapter plugin must
  pass (covers: capability declarations, IR version support,
  source-pointer resolution, registry round-trip, etc.)
- **End-to-end (per ecosystem)** — designer emits spec → adapter
  emits code → Lost Pixel matches expected baseline; runs in CI on
  every adapter change
- **Reviewer regression** — known good/bad spec/render pairs; the
  reviewer should accept the good and reject the bad
- **Designer prompt eval** — small benchmark of "feature
  description → IR" pairs; track quality across model/prompt
  changes (reuse the EL suite-test pattern from operator)

---

# 18. What we adopt vs build vs skip

**Adopt:**

- **DTCG** — token format
- **Terrazzo** (default) or **Style Dictionary** — token transformer
- **tldraw** — sketch canvas
- **Lost Pixel** — visual regression
- **Storybook** — React preview adapter (or **Ladle** if we want
  faster; revisit)
- **Figma Dev Mode MCP** — for the React/Figma mock-input adapter
- **Plotly** — chart sub-IR escape hatch
- **shadcn/ui registry-template** — as inspiration for the React
  registry adapter, not as the core schema
- **Tokens Studio for Figma** — optional human authoring path for
  DTCG
- **Adaptive Cards / Slack Block Kit** — optional export adapters
  only (not core sub-IRs)
- **OpenUI vocabulary** — as a naming reference for IR `kind` values

**Build:**

- The phase model + lifecycle gate + designer agent + reviewer
  agent
- The UI IR JSON schema (and v0.1 examples)
- The IR linter (§7.6)
- The neutral component registry schema
- The Ecosystem Adapter Contract + plugin shape
- The Design tab + 6 panes
- The `needsDesign` heuristic (reads scope text, not diffs)
- `DESIGN_SPEC.md` template + fallback chain
- React-Tailwind adapter (first; for papercusp itself)
- In-app token editor (Token inventory pane)
- Token-extraction seeder script (CSS custom properties → DTCG)
- Design lifecycle columns on
  `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated` +
  `harness_shared.harness_design_artifacts` PG table + Zero sync
  hookups (the lifecycle fields shipped as columns on the canonical
  features table, not a separate `harness_design_phase` table)

**Skip / defer:**

- **Slint syntax adoption** — JSON IR wins on agent DX and effort;
  reconsider only if humans become primary authors
- **Custom DSL parser/LSP** — see above; ~3 months of work avoided
- **Adaptive Cards as internal sub-IR** — kept only as export
  adapter
- **Vega-Lite / ECharts / ApexCharts** — Plotly chosen
- **rjsf / JSON Forms / Formily as IR concerns** — these are
  adapter implementation details
- **Penpot** — only if humans need a mock canvas later; tldraw
  covers most of it
- **Onlook** — too heavyweight to fork; reference architecture only
- **Stagewise** — dev-tool not design-tool; revisit for the review
  pass if useful
- **bolt.new / bolt.diy** — wrong altitude
- **Cross-app consistency audit pane** — defer until tokens are
  unified via DTCG

# 16. Build order

Each step is independently shippable.

1. **Schema + lifecycle fields + gate.** Add the design lifecycle
   columns (`needs_design`, `design_status`, `design_spec_id`,
   `discarded_design_work`) to the canonical features table
   `harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated`, plus the
   `harness_shared.harness_design_artifacts` table (with Zero sync).
   (Shipped as columns on the consolidated table, not a separate
   `harness_design_phase` table.) Heuristic at creation. Gate before
   implementing. No UI yet.
2. **Design tab shell** with Features pane only (mode=design).
   Three-column layout (§6.1). Validates the `mode` parameter
   abstraction.
3. **`DESIGN_SPEC.md` template + fallback chain** + designer agent
   prompt rooted in it. Designer can produce a free-form spec (no
   IR yet).
4. **UI IR v0.1** — minimal JSON Schema, hand-written examples,
   validator + linter (§7.6). Designer agent emits IR; no
   consumer yet.
5. **Ecosystem Adapter Contract** + plugin shape. Empty registry
   of adapters.
6. **`papercusp-design-react-tailwind` adapter**, capabilities:
   `registry`, `tokens` (Tailwind), `codeEmit`. Implementer agent
   prompt updated to consume IR.
7. **DTCG token store** under `design/tokens/`. Token-extraction
   seeder runs once over the operator's `harness.css` triplets to
   produce the initial DTCG file (the eat-our-own-dogfood case;
   community adapters define their own seeders). Adapter emits
   Tailwind preset + CSS vars. `harness.css` files are migrated
   incrementally (see §20.13).
8. **Component registry browser pane** (Design tab). Reads from
   the adapter.
9. **Token inventory pane** + new-token proposal flow (§9.1).
10. **Storybook preview adapter** — captures stories as examples
    for the registry; powers the preview pane.
11. **tldraw sketch pane** + artifact storage.
12. **Lost Pixel** in CI; visual regression strip pane;
    baseline-approval action (§12.1).
13. **Design memos pane** — surface existing `.mdx` memos with
    status; promote-to-feature action (§17.3).
14. **Reviewer agent + post-ship review pass** + design-crit
    agent role (§20.9).
15. **Mock-input adapters** (Figma, screenshot, tldraw-derived).
    Optional; opt-in per feature.
16. **Export adapters** (Adaptive Cards, Slack Block Kit).
    Optional; opt-in per feature.

Steps 1–4 are the spine. Steps 5–6 are the abstraction proof.
Everything after is panes and adapters that hang off the spine.

## 16.1 Rough effort estimate

- Steps 1–4 (spine): ~2–3 weeks each, sequential
- Steps 5–6 (abstraction proof): ~3–4 weeks each
- Steps 7–13 (panes + DTCG): ~1–2 weeks each, parallelizable
- Steps 14–16 (reviewer + adapters): ~2 weeks each

Total: ~2–3 months to a working v1 with the spine + React
adapter. ~6 months to feature-complete with all panes and the
reviewer loop. Add a quarter for the second ecosystem adapter to
shake out genuine ecosystem-neutrality bugs in the IR.

---

# 20. Resolved decisions

## 20.1 Model selection per role

Configurable per-harness with sensible defaults:

- Designer: best available reasoning model (Opus class)
- Crit: same family as designer (apples-to-apples comparison)
- Reviewer: mid-tier (Sonnet class) — pattern-matching task
- Implementer: unchanged from existing config

Override via `DESIGN_SPEC.md` frontmatter: `models: { designer:
"...", reviewer: "...", crit: "..." }`.

## 20.2 Adapter lifecycle and conflict

- Adapters activate lazily — on first reference (feature creation
  triggers heuristic scan; spec submission triggers code-emit)
- Manifest declares `claims: ["react-tailwind"]`; if two installed
  adapters claim the same ecosystem, harness must explicitly pick
  one in `harness.config.json` (`design.activeAdapters: { ... }`)
- Conflict surfaces as an operator directive, not a silent pick

## 20.3 Permission / sandbox model

Reuses papercusp's existing plugin permission grants. Design-phase
permissions:

- `read:registry` (always granted)
- `read:design-tokens` (always granted)
- `write:design-artifacts` (always granted for designer agents)
- `read:current-surface` (granted for redesigns)
- `propose:tokens` (granted for designer agents)
- `external-call:<targetId>` (per-export-adapter; user grants on
  install)

Adapters cannot scan paths outside their declared `sourcePaths`
without an additional grant.

## 20.4 Designer-in-flight visibility

Happy path stays out of operator directives. The feature card
shows a small "designing" badge with elapsed time + token count.
Operator directive only fires for the cases listed in §6.3
(deadlock, escalation, rejection, new-token proposal).

## 20.5 Concurrent edits / locking

- DTCG token store: optimistic locking with `version` field;
  conflicts surface a "merge needed" operator directive
- Registry entries: read-only at the IR layer (only adapters write,
  during scans, with a global advisory lock per ecosystem)
- Design specs: per-feature, no concurrent designers on one feature
  (the N=2-3 happens *before* any spec is accepted)

## 20.6 Cost telemetry per spec

Every spec artifact records `tokensIn`, `tokensOut`, `costUsd`,
`modelId`, `elapsedMs` — same shape the rest of the runtime uses.
Surfaced in the design tab's right rail per feature; aggregated in
the existing budget views.

## 20.7 Lost Pixel intentional-vs-regression

Spec acceptance writes a `targetBaselineHash` to the design phase
record. Lost Pixel diffs against the baseline; if the new hash
matches `targetBaselineHash`, the diff is auto-approved as
intended. Mismatches surface for human review. No silent baseline
drift; intent is always declared.

## 20.8 Migration of existing UI

- Existing surfaces do NOT retroactively get IR specs (the
  migration would be bottomless)
- New features: must produce IR if they create UI
- Touched features: changing an existing surface requires
  authoring its IR first (one-time cost paid lazily)
- The operator's existing surfaces become ground-truth for
  designer training data — preview adapter can capture them as
  reference material

## 20.9 Multi-designer concurrency + design crit

Hybrid; not PR-style merge.

- Orchestrator spawns 2–3 designers in parallel; each emits a
  candidate spec
- A **design-crit agent** (the reviewer agent's persona, in "crit"
  mode) scores candidates against `DESIGN_SPEC.md` rubric and
  picks ONE as canonical, optionally cherry-picking notes /
  decisions from runners-up as annotations
- Crit can deadlock (no clear winner); deadlock surfaces as an
  operator directive (§6.3) for human pick
- Auto-merging specs is a trap — design choices need a single
  authorial voice or the result is incoherent
- Default N=2; raise to 3 only when feature is high-stakes /
  orchestrator marks it `exploratory`
- Rejected candidates kept as artifacts on the feature for later
  reference, not deleted

## 20.10 IR versioning

- Schema lives in core papercusp; semver
- Every spec carries `irVersion: "0.3"`; runtime ships upgrade
  transformers between minor versions
- Adapters declare `irVersionsSupported: ["0.x", "1.x"]` in plugin
  manifest; orchestrator refuses to gate-promote a spec into an
  adapter that doesn't claim its version
- **v1.0 lock criteria:** at least 2 production adapters consuming
  IR for ≥1 month without a breaking change to the schema. Concrete
  bar; no fuzzy "mature enough."
- Ownership: core team for v1; lightweight RFC process afterward
  (the IR should stabilize fast)

## 20.11 Memo ↔ feature linkage

Promotable, with light coupling.

- Memo gets a "promote to feature" action → creates feature with
  the memo as initial spec source
- Memo retains link as `spawnedFeatures: [...]`
- Memo `status` (open / addressed / wontfix) lives on the memo
  regardless of promotion — a promoted memo flips to `addressed`
  when its feature ships
- Don't auto-promote; humans/orchestrator decide
- Un-promoted memos stay advisory and surface in the design tab's
  memo pane as backlog

## 20.12 Human override UX

No checkbox at creation (clutter). Surface override via the card
itself.

- Right-click card → "Skip design" / "Force design" — works in
  both Dashboard and Design tabs
- Keyboard shortcut for the toggle: TBD by operator UX (single-key
  shortcut conflicts likely; defer naming until Design-tab
  integration lands)
- If designer agent has already spawned, "Skip design" requires
  confirm + sets `discardedDesignWork: true` for telemetry
- Status visible on every card as a small badge (design icon when
  `needsDesign`, struck-through when manually skipped) — no extra
  rows or modals
- Heuristic should be right >90% of the time; override is an
  exception path, not first-class chrome

## 20.13 Token migration path

No magic extractor exists; we build a small one. Operator-specific
plan; community adapters define equivalents for their CSS-or-not
sources.

- **Step A — seeder script.** Regex over the three `harness.css`
  files for `:root` custom properties → DTCG seed file. Tailwind
  configs (if present) convert almost trivially because they're
  already structured.
- **Step B — manual semantic pass.** Extracted tokens have
  technical names (`--color-1`, `--space-md`); a designer (human or
  agent) renames to semantic (`color.bg.surface`, `space.gutter`)
  and dedups. This is the hard part; no tool replaces it.
- **Step C — flip the imports.** `harness.css` files become thin
  wrappers that `@import` the generated CSS vars from DTCG. Keep
  originals committed for one window.
- **Step D — Lost Pixel gate.** Run regression across known
  routes; only delete the originals when the diff is empty.
- Estimate: half a day of focused renaming for the operator
  harness; longer for libs/papercusp due to surface area.

---

# 21. Still-open questions

These remain genuinely undecided and will resolve as we hit them.

- **Designer agent failure mode:** if the designer can't produce a
  valid IR (validation fails repeatedly), does the orchestrator
  escalate to a human, fall back to free-form spec, or skip the
  phase? Probably escalate, but TBD on UI.
- **IR ↔ implementation traceability:** do generated files carry
  back-pointer comments to their source spec, or do we use a
  source-map-style sidecar (no comment noise in the code)? Lean
  sidecar.
- **Cross-harness design system sharing:** when multiple harnesses
  share a `libs/papercusp/`-equivalent, do they also share a DTCG
  store and a registry, or do those stay per-harness with explicit
  `extends` syntax in the harness's `DESIGN_SPEC.md`? Lean explicit
  `extends`, but defer until we hit the case.
- **Designer-agent web access:** can designers query the live web
  for design references (color trends, ux patterns) or are they
  closed-world to memos + registry + DESIGN_SPEC.md? Closed-world
  is safer; web access is a separate capability gate per harness.
